title: Labor backs super for all teen workers
full_text:
Young Australians under the age of 18 are closer to being paid superannuation regardless of how many hours they work, after Labor’s national conference backed the policy in a major win for the union movement.
ALP delegates committed to compulsory superannuation for teenagers as part of sweeping amendments to its 2026 policy platform at the conference in Adelaide on Thursday, including potential data-sharing between Centrelink and super funds.
The move comes less than a month after the Albanese government teamed up with the Liberals to vote down a Greens motion that would have green-lit the measure as part of payday super legislation.
Jim Chalmers did not rule out revisiting the reform at the time, but it is expected unions ramped up pressure to make an about-turn since the government blocked it with Coalition support.
The Labor policy platform has been amended to say “all workers, including those under 18 and regardless of how they are engaged, can accumulate superannuation on every dollar earned”.
Under the current scheme, teenagers are entitled to superannuation only if they work more than 30 hours a week.
Anthony Albanese and his team will now be expected to pursue a similar policy in parliament to reflect the official ALP platform, setting up a fresh fight with business in the wake of the budget.
Industry groups including the Australian Retail Council have warned against extending the entitlement, which requires employers to pay young staff an extra 12 per cent on their earnings – the rate at which the Superannuation Guarantee is paid.
NSW delegates from the Australian Services Union moved the amendment during a session on the economic tranche of Labor’s platform. The amendment was seconded by Australia’s youngest senator, Charlotte Walker, who said “not paying superannuation to under-18s is a mistake”.
“This is a chance for us to correct this,” Senator Walker said. “We know young people are often exploited in the workplace, they’re more likely to have their wages stolen from them and superannuation underpaid.
“We will always back young people at work, and we need to continue this.” At the start of the month, Labor defied calls from the ACTU and the Greens to make this reform, its payday super bill, which could have included the entitlement, exempting businesses from having to pay the entitlement to about 515,000 young Australians who qualified for the reform.
Greens spokesperson for finance, employment and workplace relations senator Barbara Pocock said then that Labor and the Liberals were robbing people.
Although unions will welcome the policy change, it could set up a new battle with the business sector while relations are still frosty, following budget reforms to capital gains tax, The party also adopted a motion from CareSuper chair Linda Scott, which was recommended by former prime minister Paul Keating, to bolster links between superannuation funds and Centrelink.
Mr Keating has argued in favour of a simplified pension system managed by super funds.
Ms Scott said Labor should close the gaps in the super system, with the adopted motion stating: “Labor will explore opportunities for secure, targeted information and data sharing between government agencies and the superannuation sector so retirees can access more accurate, timely and personalised retirement advice”. Labor also carried amendments to its national platform that recognised “inflation hurts workers and vulnerable Australians first and hardest”.
